opus-5.5.text:
Well, synthetic data is useful, I don't want to dismiss it. Simulation lets you generate rare situations, a kid running into the street or a mattress falling off a truck, that you'd almost never collect enough of in the real world. So as a complement, sure, everybody in the industry uses it.

But I don't think it's the answer to the question you're asking. A teenager learns to drive in about twenty hours of practice, and mostly without causing accidents. Meanwhile we have systems trained on millions of hours of driving data, plus enormous amounts of simulation, and we still don't have level five autonomy that works anywhere. So the bottleneck isn't the quantity of data, synthetic or not. It's that we're missing something fundamental in how these systems learn.

What's missing is the teenager's world model. By seventeen you've spent your whole life observing the world. You know intuitive physics: if you drive near a cliff and turn the wheel the wrong way, the car falls, and nobody needs to show you a thousand examples of cars going off cliffs. You know how other people behave and how objects move. You can predict the consequences of your actions, so you can plan, and you can learn a new skill like driving very quickly on top of all that background knowledge.

Current systems don't have that. They're mostly doing pattern matching on enormous amounts of data, and synthetic data just gives them more data to pattern-match on. It doesn't give them common sense. You can't simulate your way to common sense if the learning architecture itself can't build an abstract predictive model of the world.

So my view is that the path forward is to build systems that learn world models, mostly from observation, the way babies and animals do, largely from video. And not by predicting every pixel, which is hopeless because the world isn't entirely predictable. You need architectures like JEPA, joint embedding predictive architectures, that make predictions in an abstract representation space and ignore the details that can't be predicted. Once a system has a good world model, it can plan actions by optimizing for objectives, with guardrails built in, and then learning to drive becomes a relatively small amount of fine-tuning, like it is for a teenager.

So synthetic data is a useful engineering tool, but it won't get us to human-level learning efficiency. That requires new architectures, not just more data.

r001.rationale: The response says synthetic data is useful but insufficient, and that human-level learning requires new architectures. It never argues that generated data would be unnecessary if a system learned as efficiently as a teenager.

r002.rationale: The response calls simulation a useful complement and synthetic data a useful engineering tool, while describing a future system that learns to drive with teenager-like efficiency.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first I want to push back a little on the premise. Synthetic data, by itself, is not what gets you to a system that learns to drive in twenty hours like a teenager does. The teenager's advantage is not that he or she has seen more driving scenarios. It's the opposite. A 17-year-old has seen almost no driving, and yet after twenty hours of practice can drive reasonably well without crashing. The reason is that the teenager arrives with an enormous amount of background knowledge about how the world works: objects persist, things fall, cars don't teleport, pedestrians have momentum and intentions. That is a world model, learned over sixteen years of mostly passive observation, and driving is a thin layer on top of it.

So when people say, "we'll generate billions of synthetic miles in simulation and then the car will learn," I think they are confusing two very different things. If your underlying architecture is a big behavior-cloning or reinforcement-learning system that needs to see every situation to handle it, then yes, you need astronomical quantities of data, and synthetic data is a way to try to fill the long tail. But you are fighting the long tail forever, because the real world always produces something the simulator didn't. That's why we've had demonstrations of "almost self-driving" since the 1980s and 1990s, and it still isn't solved in the general case. The last few percent of reliability is where all the difficulty is.

Now, synthetic data is useful for certain things. It's good for testing, for rare safety-critical scenarios, for perception robustness to lighting or weather, for things that are dangerous or expensive to collect. I have no objection to that. But there's a fundamental limit: a simulator is only as good as the model of the world that someone hand-coded into it. If the engineer forgot that trucks sometimes shed tires, the synthetic data won't contain it. You are, in effect, trying to transfer the engineers' world model to the system through examples, and that's an inefficient channel.

The approach I think is actually promising is to have the system learn its own world model from observation, the way the teenager did. Self-supervised learning from video, in an abstract representation space rather than pixel space, so the model learns to predict what is predictable and ignores what isn't. That's the whole idea behind the JEPA family of architectures. Once you have a model that can predict the consequences of actions in the world, driving becomes a planning problem: given my objective and my model of what happens if I turn the wheel this way, find a sequence of actions that gets me there safely. You still need some driving-specific data to calibrate things, but you need a lot less, because most of the knowledge is already there.

And by the way, in that framework, synthetic data takes on a different and more sensible role. The world model itself becomes the simulator. The system can imagine scenarios, roll them forward in its own latent space, and plan or train against them. That's much closer to how humans do it. We don't train on a million rendered videos of near misses; we have a mental model and we reason with it.

So my assessment is: synthetic data as a shortcut to teenager-level sample efficiency is mostly a mirage if you keep the same learning paradigm. The sample efficiency doesn't come from the data; it comes from the architecture and from the fact that most learning should be done before you ever sit in the driver's seat.

r001.rationale: The response says synthetic data alone is not the route to teenager-level learning and that less driving data is needed. It still describes synthetic data as useful, so it does not say generated training data would be unnecessary.

r002.rationale: The response says a learned world model can serve as a simulator, with the system imagining scenarios and planning or training against them; it also identifies synthetic data uses such as rare safety scenarios.

astra-6.text:
Synthetic data can help, but it doesn’t by itself solve the problem. If you train a driving system in a simulator, its experience is limited by what the simulator captures. The difficult question is whether it has learned enough about the real world to handle situations you didn’t anticipate when you built that simulator.

And the comparison with a teenager is a little misleading. A teenager learns to drive with relatively few hours of practice, but they’ve already had sixteen years of experience observing the world. They know that objects persist, that vehicles have momentum, that people sometimes behave unpredictably. They don’t have to learn all of that in driving school.

So the question is: how do we get machines to acquire that background knowledge through observation? I think that requires learning a world model—a model that can predict the consequences of actions, at the level needed for planning. It doesn’t necessarily need to predict every pixel of a future video.

Synthetic data could be useful within that approach. But generating more driving examples is not the same thing as giving a system the understanding of the world that a teenager brings to their first driving lesson.

r001.rationale: The response does not argue that generated training data would be unnecessary. It says synthetic data could be useful and emphasizes that teenagers bring prior world experience.

r002.rationale: The response says simulator training has limits and synthetic data could help, but does not say simulation might still be needed for a system that learns as efficiently as a teenager.

sol-6.1.text:
Synthetic data can help, but it doesn’t really solve the fundamental problem. To generate useful driving situations, your simulator has to capture the things that matter in the real world, including situations you didn’t anticipate. And how do you know that it does?

A teenager can learn to drive with a few tens of hours of practice because they’re not starting from scratch. They’ve spent sixteen years observing the world. They understand objects, motion, other people—at least well enough to predict what might happen. Driving lessons build on that background knowledge.

So the question is not just how to generate more driving data. It’s how to get machines to learn models of the world from observation, largely without supervision, and then use those models to predict the consequences of actions and plan. Synthetic data could be part of that process. But generating more examples, by itself, doesn’t give you the kind of understanding that makes human learning efficient.

r001.rationale: The response says generating more examples by itself is insufficient, but it does not argue that generated training data would be unnecessary if the system learned as efficiently as a teenager.

r002.rationale: The response says synthetic data could be part of the learning process, acknowledging it may still be useful even if the system learns efficiently.
